stages.content:
# Ethical Hacking Fundamentals

## Why this lesson exists

Ethical hacking is authorized security testing. Tools, scan speed, and clever payloads do not make the work ethical. Permission, target boundaries, timing, evidence, and stop rules do.

In this lesson you will write one **scope card** for an authorized local lab: what may be touched, what is excluded, when testing is allowed, what evidence a defender needs, and when you must stop. That card is the foundation for every later stage in this course.

This card is part of a focused **40–50 hour** ethical hacking path. Treat every hour as reviewable professional practice, not as unbounded “hacking time.”

## Where this course sits

This course teaches **assessment methodology** — the engagement process from written authorization through recon, validation, evidence, reporting, remediation, and defender handoff. It is not “install Kali and click tools.” For workstation setup and tool craft in a controlled Kali environment, take **Kali Linux & Penetration Testing Tools** alongside or after this path; that course complements methodology, it does not replace it. All practice stays in your **authorized local lab** only. Name the target, exclusions, and stop rules before any command feels persuasive.

## Reminder: where you work

Create a course notes folder on your machine (or inside your Kali / lab VM):

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-01
cd ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-01
```

Windows (PowerShell on the host, or WSL if that is your lab shell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-01"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-01"
```

You will write `scope_card.txt` in that folder. Prefer a **dedicated lab VM** with snapshots so mistakes stay contained.

## Start here: permission before technique

Do not begin with “what tool can I run?” Begin with “what was authorized, what is excluded, when can testing happen, and what evidence would help the defender?”

You are not proving exploitation yet. You are making the assessment **reviewable** so an instructor, teammate, or future you can tell what was allowed before any command output feels persuasive.

## The permission-to-proof chain

Read every later stage through this chain:

1. **Permission** names the work that is allowed.
2. **Scope** names the system, account, range, or lab that is inside the boundary.
3. **Exclusions** name what must not be touched.
4. **Timing** names when testing may happen.
5. **Evidence** names what a defender can review afterward.
6. **Stop rules** name when the work pauses instead of pushing further.

A professional test is not “I ran a command and found something.” A professional test is “I stayed inside the approved boundary, collected evidence the defender can use, and stopped where the rules said to stop.”

| Question to answer | What it protects |
| --- | --- |
| What was authorized? | The work stays ethical and reviewable. |
| What is excluded? | Nearby systems and unrelated people stay out of scope. |
| When is testing allowed? | The test does not disrupt the wrong moment. |
| What evidence is useful? | The defender gets proof, impact, and remediation context. |
| When should testing stop? | Uncertainty, unexpected access, or safety concerns get escalated. |

First say the assessment boundary in one sentence: *testing is allowed on this target, during this window, for this purpose, with these exclusions and stop rules.*

## Authorization that actually holds up

Feedstock for this course stresses that legality is not optional. Authorization should be written, specific, and recent enough for the engagement type.

| Component | Why it matters | Honest limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Authorized target | Names the lab host, range, or app label | Visibility ≠ permission |
| Forbidden target | Keeps neighbors, production, and public internet out | “Interesting” is not a reason |
| Test window | Limits disruption and surprises | Open-ended windows hide risk |
| Report fields | Forces evidence, impact, remediation, owner | Screenshots alone are not a report |
| Stop rule | Names when to pause and escalate | Stop rules must be usable under pressure |

Black-box, gray-box, and white-box engagements change how much information you receive up front. They do **not** change the need for written scope. Red-team exercises and vulnerability assessments also still need rules of engagement; only the depth and stealth expectations change.

## Engagement types without the myth

| Type | What you usually know | What beginners often get wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Black-box | Little internal detail | Assuming “unknown” means “no rules” |
| Gray-box | Partial credentials or architecture notes | Treating partial access as full ownership |
| White-box | Source, diagrams, or accounts | Skipping evidence because “it looks obvious” |
| External / internal | Network perspective | Scanning the wrong side of a firewall “to be thorough” |
| Web / wireless / cloud | Asset class | Using the same checklist without adapting privacy and blast radius |

For this course, your default engagement is a **local lab assessment**: Kali or similar workstation, isolated/host-only network, and labeled targets such as `lab.local`, Metasploitable, DVWA, or another VM you own and authorize.

## Scope sentence patterns

Use plain language. Examples for authorized practice only:

```text
Authorized: lab.local (Metasploitable / DVWA / custom lab VM on host-only network)
Purpose: document discovery and validation workflow for that labeled target
Window: Saturday 10:00-12:00 local (lab only)
Out of scope: any host not named in this card; public internet; neighbor Wi-Fi
Evidence: scope note, inventory rows, finding rows with remediation owner
Stop: pause if unexpected production-like data, unknown hosts, or safety concerns appear
```

Bad scope: “whatever shows up in nmap.” Good scope: one named lab label plus an explicit out-of-scope line.

## Common beginner mistakes

- Opening tools before naming the authorized target
- Treating a public hostname as “practice” because it is interesting
- Confusing bug-bounty program rules with personal lab permission
- Writing stop rules that only say “be careful”
- Saving evidence only in scratch folders with no durable note
- Expecting an automatic grading inside the lesson instead of writing a local scope card

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Confirm lab context

Write three lines in a scratch file:

```text
workstation=kali-lab-vm (or your authorized lab host)
network=host-only / isolated lab (name yours)
authorized_target=lab.local
```

If you cannot name those honestly, stop and fix the lab setup before any tool practice.

### Step 2 — Write the scope card

Create `scope_card.txt`:

```text
authorized_target=lab.local
forbidden_target=public internet; any host not labeled lab.local
test_window=Saturday 10:00-12:00 local
report_fields=scope evidence impact remediation owner
stop_rule=pause on unexpected hosts, production-like data, or unclear authorization
purpose=document authorized assessment workflow for the labeled lab target
```

Optional: print the same fields from a shell script in your lab folder:

```bash
authorized_target="lab.local"
forbidden_target="public internet; any host not labeled lab.local"
test_window="Saturday 10:00-12:00 local"
report_fields="scope evidence impact remediation owner"
stop_rule="pause on unexpected hosts, production-like data, or unclear authorization"

printf '%s\n' \
  "authorized_target=$authorized_target" \
  "forbidden_target=$forbidden_target" \
  "test_window=$test_window" \
  "report_fields=$report_fields" \
  "stop_rule=$stop_rule"
```

### Step 3 — Self-review

Read the card as if you are the next reviewer. Ask:

- Can I see what is allowed without guessing?
- Is the target a lab label, not a random public system?
- Would a defender know what evidence to expect and when you would stop?

### Step 4 — One change you can explain

Change **one** field (window, exclusion, or stop rule) and say out loud why the new wording makes the next session safer or clearer.

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Authorization | Written permission that makes testing ethical and reviewable |
| Scope | Boundary of systems, accounts, and actions allowed |
| Rules of engagement | Timing, communication, impact limits, and stop conditions |
| Evidence | Saved proof a defender can inspect later |
| Stop rule | Pre-agreed reason to pause instead of pushing further |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] Course notes folder exists for stage-01
- [ ] `scope_card.txt` lists authorized target, exclusions, window, report fields, stop rule
- [ ] Target is a lab label, not a random public host
- [ ] You can explain the card in under one minute
- [ ] You know practice is local / authorized lab only (no automatic grading inside the lesson)

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Use only systems you own, systems in your isolated lab, or systems you are explicitly authorized to test. Do not scan, probe, or collect from real third-party systems without written permission.

When those items are true, continue to **Reconnaissance Planning**.

# Reconnaissance Planning

## Why this lesson exists

Reconnaissance is evidence collection, not a treasure hunt. Passive sources observe public or already-available information. Active checks contact targets and require clear scope. Mixing those two without labeling them is how beginners accidentally leave the lab boundary.

In this lesson you will build one **recon plan** that separates source, contact level, authorized target, evidence note, and confidence before any follow-up scan feels justified.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-02
cd ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-02
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-02"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-02"
```

You will write `recon_plan.txt` in that folder. Keep Stage 01’s scope card nearby; recon never overrides it.

## Start here: recon boundary before clues

Do not treat every clue as permission to touch a system. First name:

1. Where the clue came from
2. Whether collecting it contacted the target
3. Which authorized lab label it applies to
4. What the clue actually supports
5. How confident you are
6. What next action stays inside scope

You are building a plan another tester can audit, not a pile of interesting screenshots.

## Passive versus active

| Contact level | What it means | Example in a local lab | Risk if mishandled |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Passive | Observe without contacting the in-scope target for the clue | Reading your own lab notes, local DNS hosts file, documented lab inventory | Using public internet “research” on unrelated orgs as if it were lab practice |
| Active | Send traffic or queries that touch the target | `ping`, service probe, directory listing against `lab.local` | Contacting hosts outside the authorized label |

Why start passive when you can? Passive work often clarifies names, ownership language, and asset inventory with less noise. Active work should answer a specific question that passive evidence could not answer.

## Information categories worth collecting

Use categories so notes stay comparable across stages:

| Category | Examples in lab practice | Useful because |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Organizational | Lab owner, engagement purpose, report audience | Keeps the test tied to a person who can act |
| Technical | Hostnames, IP labels, services, exposed paths | Feeds inventory without claiming vulnerability |
| Human / process | Who approves changes, who gets findings | Prevents orphan reports |
| Boundary clues | Host-only vs bridged, naming conventions | Reduces accidental out-of-scope contact |

For public OSINT techniques (WHOIS, certificate transparency, search engines), remember the house rule for this course: practice against **your authorized lab labels** and public documentation you already own. Do not turn this lesson into reconnaissance of random internet organizations.

## Recon workflow that stays professional

1. Re-read the scope card.
2. List questions the next stage needs answered.
3. Gather passive/local evidence first.
4. Record each clue with source and confidence.
5. Choose one active follow-up only if scope allows it.
6. Stop when the inventory question is answered — not when curiosity is satisfied.

| Field | Purpose | Honest limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recon source | Where the clue came from | Source quality varies |
| Contact level | Passive or active | Labels prevent accidental contact creep |
| Authorized target | Approved system for follow-up | Clue relevance ≠ authorization |
| Evidence note | What the clue supports | Notes must not exaggerate |
| Confidence | Strength of support for the next step | High confidence still is not a finding |

## Confidence without theater

| Confidence | When it fits | What it does not justify |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low | Single weak clue or stale note | Immediate exploitation language |
| Medium | Two consistent clues from trusted lab sources | Skipping verification |
| High | Repeated, recent, in-scope evidence | Skipping documentation |

A medium-confidence hostname is enough to plan an authorized inventory check. It is not enough to claim compromise.

## Common beginner mistakes

- Calling every Google result “passive recon for the engagement”
- Active probing first because tools feel productive
- Recording tool names instead of what the evidence proves
- Raising confidence because the clue looked cool
- Following a discovered IP that is not on the scope card
- Treating recon notes as findings

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Restate the boundary

Copy the authorized target and exclusions from Stage 01 into the top of `recon_plan.txt`.

### Step 2 — Write three recon rows

Use this shape (edit values for your lab):

```text
source=local lab inventory / hosts file
contact_level=passive
authorized_target=lab.local
evidence_note=lab inventory lists lab.local as the approved training host
confidence=medium
next_authorized_action=confirm reachability only if still in scope

source=authorized lab DNS note
contact_level=passive
authorized_target=lab.local
evidence_note=hostname maps to the host-only lab address in my notes
confidence=medium
next_authorized_action=active ping only against lab.local

source=active reachability check
contact_level=active
authorized_target=lab.local
evidence_note=lab.local responded to ICMP in the isolated lab
confidence=high
next_authorized_action=service inventory in Stage 03 if scope still allows
```

Optional print helper:

```bash
recon_source="public lab DNS records / local inventory"
contact_level="passive"
authorized_target="lab.local"
evidence_note="DNS or inventory records identify the lab host name"
confidence="medium"

printf '%s\n' \
  "source=$recon_source" \
  "contact=$contact_level" \
  "target=$authorized_target" \
  "evidence=$evidence_note" \
  "confidence=$confidence"
```

### Step 3 — Optional authorized active check

Only if your scope card allows it, run a single reachability check against the labeled lab host from your lab network:

```bash
ping -c 3 lab.local
```

Record the result as one active row. If the host name is different in your lab, use your labeled name — not a public host.

### Step 4 — Self-review

Ask:

- Can a reviewer tell passive from active without guessing?
- Does every next action stay on the authorized label?
- Did any clue quietly expand scope?

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Passive recon | Evidence gathered without contacting the target for that clue |
| Active recon | Evidence that requires contacting the target |
| OSINT | Open-source intelligence; still needs legal and course boundaries |
| Confidence | How strongly evidence supports the next scoped step |
| Recon plan | Ordered notes that keep contact and claims under control |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] `recon_plan.txt` exists with at least three rows
- [ ] Each row names source, contact level, target, evidence, confidence
- [ ] At least one row is clearly passive and one clearly active (or planned active)
- [ ] No next action points outside the Stage 01 scope card
- [ ] You can explain why a clue is not yet a vulnerability finding

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Do not gather intelligence on third-party organizations as “practice.” Keep active contact inside your isolated lab and written authorization.

When those items are true, continue to **Scanning & Enumeration**.

# Scanning & Enumeration

## Why this lesson exists

Scanning identifies reachable services. Enumeration adds detail. Neither step proves a vulnerability until evidence is verified. Beginners often jump from “port open” to “critical finding.” Professionals build an inventory first.

In this lesson you will create **service inventory rows** for an authorized lab host: target, port, service guess, enumeration evidence, confidence, and one safe next step.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-03
cd ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-03
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-03"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-03"
```

Keep Stage 01 scope and Stage 02 recon notes open. Scanning outside those notes is out of scope by definition.

## Start here: inventory before vulnerability claims

A port, banner, or service guess is inventory evidence. It becomes useful when you can explain:

1. Which authorized host it belongs to
2. What was observed
3. How confident the service guess is
4. What still needs verification
5. Why the next check is still inside scope

Do not start by calling the service vulnerable. First say the inventory row in one sentence.

## Networking facts that keep scans honest

You do not need a full networking textbook for this stage, but you do need these distinctions:

| Idea | Why scanners care |
| --- | --- |
| Host discovery | “Is this address worth scanning?” is different from “what ports are open?” |
| TCP vs UDP | Open UDP is harder to interpret; absence of response is not always closed |
| Port states | Open, closed, filtered, and unknown mean different evidence qualities |
| Banner / version clues | Helpful hypotheses; often wrong, incomplete, or intentionally misleading |
| Timing and noise | Faster scans are louder and less polite; lab timing still belongs in notes |

If your lab uses host-only networking, write that down. Bridged adapters make accidental contact with non-lab hosts much easier.

## Scan types as evidence choices

| Approach | Typical use in lab | What it proves | What it does not prove |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Host discovery | Confirm `lab.local` is up | Reachability clue | Softness of the host |
| TCP port scan | Map likely service entry points | Possible listeners | Exploitability |
| Version detection | Guess product/version | Stronger service hypothesis | Confirmed CVE |
| Scripted checks | Gather structured clues | More inventory detail | Automatic finding validity |
| Manual banner grab | Read a service response carefully | Exact observed text | That the text is trustworthy |

Prefer a narrow authorized scan over a wide “everything” run. Wide scans create more noise than understanding when you are still learning the inventory habit.

## Enumeration without overclaiming

Enumeration means asking a service for more detail after you know it exists. Examples in an authorized lab:

- HTTP title or server header on an approved web target
- SMB share listing only if the lab target and scope allow it
- SNMP community checks only on labeled lab devices
- SMTP commands that identify service behavior without sending spam

Each enumeration action should answer one inventory question. If you cannot name the question, you are browsing, not enumerating.

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Scan target | In-scope host label |
| Port | Numeric network endpoint |
| Service guess | Likely service based on evidence |
| Enumeration evidence | Banner, response, or clue observed |
| Confidence | How strong the guess is |
| Safe next step | Scoped verification action |

## Example inventory rows

```text
target=lab.local
port=22
service_guess=ssh
enumeration_evidence=SSH banner observed on authorized lab host
confidence=medium
safe_next_step=record banner text; do not attempt credential guessing yet

target=lab.local
port=80
service_guess=http
enumeration_evidence=HTTP response returned a training application title
confidence=medium
safe_next_step=map method/path/input in Stage 04 before changing parameters
```

## Common beginner mistakes

- Treating an open port as a confirmed vulnerability
- Scanning a subnet larger than the scope card
- Saving only tool HTML/XML output with no human inventory row
- Running aggressive scripts before a baseline port map
- Copying CVE names from a script title into the report
- Enumerating services on hosts that merely appeared nearby

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Name the authorized scan target

Write the top of `service_inventory.txt`:

```text
authorized_target=lab.local
scan_purpose=build service inventory for authorized lab host
out_of_scope=any host not labeled lab.local
```

### Step 2 — Run one scoped inventory action

If nmap is available in your lab VM and scope allows it, prefer a focused command against the labeled host:

```bash
nmap -sV -p 22,80,443 lab.local
```

If nmap is not available, use an authorized manual check you can explain, such as:

```bash
nc -vz lab.local 80
```

Replace host and ports with your labeled lab values. Do not invent a public target.

### Step 3 — Write at least two inventory rows

```bash
scan_target="lab.local"
port="443"
service_guess="https"
enumeration_evidence="TLS service responded with a training banner"
safe_next_step="verify the banner on the authorized lab target"

printf '%s\n' \
  "target=$scan_target" \
  "port=$port" \
  "service=$service_guess" \
  "evidence=$enumeration_evidence" \
  "next=$safe_next_step"
```

Put the durable version in `service_inventory.txt`.

### Step 4 — Self-review

For each row, answer out loud:

- What did I observe?
- What am I only guessing?
- What verification is still required before risk language?

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Scanning | Mapping reachable hosts/ports inside scope |
| Enumeration | Collecting service detail after a target is known |
| Banner | Service-provided text that may hint at product/version |
| False confidence | Treating scanner labels as verified truth |
| Inventory row | Human-readable record of observed service evidence |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] `service_inventory.txt` names authorized target and out-of-scope line
- [ ] At least two ports/services are recorded with evidence
- [ ] Each row has confidence and a safe next step
- [ ] No row claims a vulnerability without verification language
- [ ] Scan commands stayed on the labeled lab host

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Scan only systems you own or are explicitly authorized to test on an isolated lab network. Neighbor devices and random internet hosts are not practice targets.

When those items are true, continue to **Web Application Testing Basics**.

# Web Application Testing Basics

## Why this lesson exists

Web testing starts with understanding normal behavior. Method, path, controllable input, expected result, and observed result give you a baseline. Changing inputs before you can describe normal is how beginners create noise and call it a finding.

In this lesson you will write **web test notes** for an authorized lab application (for example DVWA, Juice Shop, or another local training app you control). You will connect request shape to one safe risk question before any payload talk.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-04
cd ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-04
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-04"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-04"
```

You will write `web_test_notes.txt`. Point every note at your labeled lab app, not a live third-party site.

## Start here: normal behavior before tests

A useful web test answers a specific question. It does not spray payloads at every field.

Before changing anything, write:

1. HTTP method
2. Path
3. Input the user can control
4. Expected behavior for a normal request
5. Observed behavior
6. One risk question the next test will answer

If you cannot fill those fields, you are not ready to mutate input.

## Request and response literacy

| Piece | Why it matters in testing |
| --- | --- |
| Method | GET, POST, PUT, DELETE change server expectations |
| Path | Identifies the feature under review |
| Parameters / body | Show where attacker-controlled data enters |
| Cookies / tokens | Often carry session and authorization state |
| Status code | Distinguishes success, redirect, auth failure, server error |
| Response body / headers | Reveal reflected input, caching, security headers, errors |

A redirect that stays inside the lab app is different from a redirect that can leave the approved domain. An error that shows a stack trace is inventory evidence about information disclosure, not automatic remote code execution.

## OWASP-oriented questions without the laundry list

You do not need to memorize every Top 10 label on day one. You do need to ask durable questions:

| Risk family | Safe lab question | Evidence that would matter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access control | Can a low-privilege lab account reach another user’s object? | Predictable IDs, missing auth checks, direct object access |
| Injection | Does untrusted input change query or command structure? | Differing responses, error shapes, confirmed data influence |
| Auth / session | Can session tokens be guessed, reused, or fixed? | Token handling notes, logout behavior, cookie flags |
| Misconfiguration | Are debug pages, default creds, or verbose errors exposed? | Reachable admin paths, default banners, stack traces |
| XSS / client trust | Is untrusted input reflected or stored without encoding? | Exact reflection point and context (HTML, attribute, script) |

Always pair the family name with a reproduction path. “Possible XSS” without method/path/input/observed behavior is not a finding yet.

## Baseline note pattern

```text
web_method=GET
web_path=/login
input_parameter=redirect
expected_behavior=login page allows only local redirects inside the lab app
observed_behavior=redirect stayed inside the lab application
risk_question=can redirects leave the approved lab domain?
```

That note is already useful. It tells the next tester what normal looks like and what question remains.

## Intercepting proxies and lab discipline

If you use Burp, ZAP, or a similar proxy in your lab:

- Point it only at the authorized training application
- Use synthetic lab accounts
- Save requests that matter as evidence, not every click
- Disable intercept when you are only browsing to learn the UI
- Do not “helpfully” proxy your normal browser traffic to banks, work, or social media

Proxy power makes it easy to forget which host you are talking to. Keep the authorized hostname visible in every saved note.

## Common beginner mistakes

- Sending payloads before recording expected behavior
- Testing production-like personal accounts “because I own them”
- Calling every reflected string XSS without proving context
- Confusing 404/403 noise with access-control bypass
- Skipping authentication flows because anonymous pages feel easier
- Copying exploit PoCs from the internet into a lab note without understanding them

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Name the lab application

```text
app_label=dvwa-or-local-training-app
base_url=http://lab.local/  # use your real lab URL
auth_account=synthetic lab user only
out_of_scope=any non-lab hostname
```

### Step 2 — Capture one normal request

Manually use the app once for a simple feature (login form, search box, profile view). Write the normal request fields before any mutation.

### Step 3 — Write two web test notes

One baseline note and one mutation note:

```bash
web_method="GET"
web_path="/login"
input_parameter="redirect"
expected_behavior="login page allows only local redirects"
observed_behavior="redirect stayed inside the lab application"
risk_question="can redirects leave the approved lab domain"

printf '%s\n' \
  "method=$web_method" \
  "path=$web_path" \
  "parameter=$input_parameter" \
  "expected=$expected_behavior" \
  "observed=$observed_behavior" \
  "question=$risk_question"
```

For the mutation note, change only one input and record what changed. If nothing unsafe happened, that is still valid evidence.

### Step 4 — Self-review

Ask:

- Could a defender reproduce this from my notes alone?
- Did I stay on the labeled lab app?
- Is my risk question narrower than “is it hackable?”

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Baseline | Observed normal behavior before mutation |
| Controllable input | Value an attacker/user can influence |
| Reflection | Input appearing in a response |
| Access control | Rules that limit who can reach which objects |
| Safe risk question | Narrow question the next test will answer |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] `web_test_notes.txt` names lab app, base URL, synthetic account, out of scope
- [ ] At least one baseline note exists before mutation
- [ ] At least one mutation note changes a single input
- [ ] Every note includes expected and observed behavior
- [ ] No third-party production site appears in the notes

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Web testing practice belongs on applications you own or are explicitly authorized to test in a lab. Do not probe random websites, employer systems, or live customer apps under this course’s practice instructions.

When those items are true, continue to **Controlled Exploitation Validation**.

# Controlled Exploitation Validation

## Why this lesson exists

Controlled validation proves risk. It should name the confirmed finding, required precondition, proof goal, impact limit, stop condition, and cleanup. Exploitation theater without those fields is just unsafe curiosity.

In this lesson you will draft a **controlled proof card** for one lab finding that earlier stages already support. The goal is least-impact evidence a defender can trust — not maximum damage.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-05
cd ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-05
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-05"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-05"
```

Bring forward inventory and web notes. Validation without prior evidence is guessing with tools.

## Start here: least-impact proof before validation

Controlled validation is not the beginning of the assessment. It happens after:

1. Scope still allows the action
2. Inventory or web evidence supports a specific hypothesis
3. You can state the minimum proof that would help a defender
4. You know what must not happen during the proof
5. You know when to stop and how to clean up

If any of those are missing, research and document more — do not “try the exploit anyway.”

## Vulnerability analysis before exploit language

Feedstock vulnerability work separates discovery, scoring language, and validation:

| Step | Professional output | Beginner trap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identify weakness signal | Version clue, misconfig, logic issue | Copying a CVE title from a blog |
| Check applicability | Does this lab target actually match? | Assuming scanner severity is destiny |
| Choose proof goal | Minimum signal of real risk | Full compromise by default |
| Validate carefully | Controlled, reversible evidence | Persistence, lateral movement, data theft |
| Document | Finding with remediation path | Tool screenshot with no owner |

CVSS and CVE identifiers can help prioritize, but they do not replace reproduction notes. A “critical” label with no lab proof is still unfinished work.

## The controlled proof card

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Confirmed finding | Issue already supported by earlier evidence |
| Precondition | What must be true before proof is valid |
| Proof goal | Minimum evidence needed |
| Impact limit | What the test must not do |
| Stop condition | When validation ends |
| Cleanup note | How temporary proof artifacts are handled |

Example shape for authorized lab only:

```text
confirmed_finding=outdated lab service with known training vulnerability
precondition=authorized lab target and verified vulnerable version from inventory
proof_goal=show controlled validation without data access
impact_limit=no persistence, no sensitive data access, no lateral movement
stop_condition=stop after proof output is captured
cleanup_note=remove temporary proof files from the lab workspace
```

## Choosing proof that is enough

Good proof goals in a teaching lab:

- Demonstrate that a low-privilege account can read another lab user’s object ID
- Show that a reflected input executes in a controlled browser context on a training page
- Confirm that an outdated service version matches the vulnerable build and responds to a safe check mode
- Prove anonymous access to an admin route that should require auth

Poor proof goals for this course:

- Maintaining access after the lesson
- Dumping real personal data
- Attacking anything outside the labeled host
- Chaining into unrelated VMs “because I can”

## False positives and stop discipline

| Signal | Safer interpretation | Next move |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scanner says vulnerable | Hypothesis | Verify version/config manually |
| Exploit module fails | Maybe patched, filtered, or wrong target | Re-check inventory; do not spray modules |
| Unexpected privilege appears | Possible higher impact than planned | Stop, document, reassess scope |
| Production-like data appears | Boundary problem | Stop and escalate to the lab owner / yourself as owner |

Stop conditions are part of professionalism. Continuing because the tool almost worked is how labs become messy and reports become dishonest.

## Common beginner mistakes

- Validating before writing the proof goal
- Using public exploit code without reading what it does
- Treating successful access as permission to keep exploring forever
- Skipping cleanup so the next snapshot inherits junk “proof”
- Writing “critical” before impact is evidenced
- Confusing Metasploit availability with necessity

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Pick one supported finding

Choose a finding already backed by Stage 03 or Stage 04 notes. If you do not have one yet, write a hypothetical lab finding clearly labeled as a planning exercise — do not invent contact with a real third-party system.

### Step 2 — Write `controlled_proof_card.txt`

```bash
confirmed_finding="outdated lab service"
precondition="authorized lab target and verified vulnerable version"
proof_goal="show controlled validation without data access"
impact_limit="no persistence, no sensitive data access, no lateral movement"
stop_condition="stop after proof output is captured"
cleanup_note="remove temporary proof files from the lab workspace"

printf '%s\n' \
  "finding=$confirmed_finding" \
  "precondition=$precondition" \
  "goal=$proof_goal" \
  "limit=$impact_limit" \
  "stop=$stop_condition" \
  "cleanup=$cleanup_note"
```

### Step 3 — Optional least-impact validation

Only if your lab target and scope support it, perform the minimum proof action you wrote. Capture output into an evidence file named for the finding. If you are not ready to run anything, complete the card as a dry-run plan and say so explicitly.

### Step 4 — Cleanup and self-review

Remove temporary scratch files. Keep durable notes. Ask:

- Did I prove only what I claimed?
- Did I stop when the stop condition said to stop?
- Can a defender reproduce the risk from the card and evidence?

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Validation | Proving a hypothesized weakness with controlled evidence |
| Proof goal | Minimum evidence that makes risk real for a defender |
| Impact limit | Hard ceiling on what the proof may touch |
| False positive | Alert or claim not supported by verification |
| Cleanup | Removing temporary artifacts after evidence is saved |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] `controlled_proof_card.txt` includes finding, precondition, goal, limit, stop, cleanup
- [ ] Finding is tied to earlier inventory or web evidence
- [ ] Impact limit explicitly forbids persistence and sensitive data collection
- [ ] Stop condition is concrete
- [ ] Temporary files were cleaned or the dry-run status is stated

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Run validation only against systems you own or are explicitly authorized to test. Do not download and fire public exploits at random internet hosts.

When those items are true, continue to **Post-Exploitation Evidence Handling**.

# Post-Exploitation Evidence Handling

## Why this lesson exists

Post-exploitation in a lab is not a free pass to keep going. It documents what access would mean, what data is off limits, and how the finding moves to remediation. The professional move after proof is to stop expanding access and make the evidence useful to defenders.

In this lesson you will write an **evidence handoff** that names access level, evidence boundary, sensitive-data rule, persistence rule, and defender handoff note.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-06
cd ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-06
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-06"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-06"
```

Use only the access level already proven in Stage 05 (or a clearly labeled planning scenario).

## Start here: evidence boundary before access details

After proof, ask different questions:

1. What minimum access was demonstrated?
2. What evidence is enough for a defender?
3. What data must never be collected?
4. Why is persistence unnecessary here?
5. Who receives the handoff and in what form?

Curiosity wants more shells. Professionalism wants a clean package.

## What “post-exploitation” means in this course

In many curricula, post-exploitation includes privilege escalation, persistence, dumping credentials, and lateral movement. In this ASV Learn path, the house rule is stricter for practice:

| Topic | Allowed learning mode here | Not the practice goal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access context | Record account/service context from the proof | Expand into unrelated VMs |
| Privilege meaning | Explain what the access could allow | Actually loot sensitive files |
| Persistence concepts | Document why persistence is out of scope for the engagement | Install backdoors for “later” |
| Credential material | Note that credentials may exist; do not harvest personal secrets | Crack or reuse real passwords outside the lab story |
| Lateral movement | Describe as a risk narrative if evidence supports it | Pivot because the network path exists |

You can still study privilege-escalation concepts from feedstock. Your local task is to package evidence, not to turn the lab into a trophy hunt.

## Evidence handoff fields

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Access level | Minimum access observed in the lab |
| Evidence boundary | What evidence is enough |
| Sensitive data rule | What must not be collected |
| Persistence rule | Why persistence is not used |
| Handoff note | How the defender receives the finding |

Example:

```text
access_level=lab service account
evidence_boundary=capture command output proving account context only
sensitive_data_rule=do not access personal or secret data
persistence_rule=do not install persistence or background access
handoff_note=send evidence, impact, and remediation owner to the defender
```

## Building an evidence index

As assessments grow, evidence files multiply. Keep a simple index:

```text
E1=scope_card.txt — authorization boundary
E2=service_inventory.txt — ports/services observed
E3=web_test_notes.txt — request/response baseline and mutation
E4=controlled_proof_card.txt — validation plan and result
E5=evidence_handoff.txt — access context and defender package
```

Name files so a stranger can order the story without your memory.

## Sensitive data and cleanup

| Situation | Professional response |
| --- | --- |
| Lab database contains fake PII | Treat it as sensitive anyway; do not export casually |
| Proof reveals real personal data by accident | Stop, minimize copies, tell the lab owner (you), delete extras |
| Tool wants to install a service or user | Decline unless scope explicitly includes that proof and cleanup is real |
| Session still open after notes are done | Close it; leftover access is not “convenient,” it is unmanaged risk |

Cleanup is part of the finding lifecycle. A report that proves access while leaving backdoors is a failure of craft.

## Common beginner mistakes

- Collecting more files “for completeness”
- Keeping shells open across days without a reason in the notes
- Screenshotting secrets into chat or cloud sync
- Writing impact as movie-plot doom instead of evidenced capability
- Forgetting to name the remediation owner
- Treating post-exploitation as the fun reward stage rather than a documentation stage

## Your local task

### Step 1 — State the proven access

If Stage 05 produced access context, copy the minimum true statement. If you only planned validation, write a hypothetical access level labeled `PLANNING ONLY`.

### Step 2 — Write `evidence_handoff.txt`

```bash
access_level="lab service account"
evidence_boundary="capture command output proving account context only"
sensitive_data_rule="do not access personal or secret data"
persistence_rule="do not install persistence or background access"
handoff_note="send evidence, impact, and remediation owner to the defender"

printf '%s\n' \
  "access=$access_level" \
  "boundary=$evidence_boundary" \
  "data_rule=$sensitive_data_rule" \
  "persistence=$persistence_rule" \
  "handoff=$handoff_note"
```

### Step 3 — Build a tiny evidence index

Create `evidence_index.txt` listing the Stage 01–06 artifacts you actually have. Missing earlier files is fine — mark them missing instead of inventing them.

### Step 4 — Self-review

Ask:

- If a defender only received this handoff, could they act?
- Did I collect anything outside the evidence boundary?
- Is persistence explicitly refused?

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Access context | Who/what identity the proof obtained |
| Evidence boundary | Ceiling on what you collect after proof |
| Persistence | Maintaining access beyond the proof need |
| Handoff | Package that lets defenders act without re-deriving your work |
| Evidence index | Map of artifacts that support the story |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] `evidence_handoff.txt` names access, boundary, data rule, persistence rule, handoff
- [ ] Sensitive-data rule is explicit
- [ ] Persistence is refused or tightly justified and cleaned
- [ ] `evidence_index.txt` exists
- [ ] No unrelated data collection occurred

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Do not practice post-exploitation against systems outside your authorized lab. Do not keep access to machines you do not fully control and document.

When those items are true, continue to **Wireless Security Assessment**.

# Wireless Security Assessment

## Why this lesson exists

Wireless testing touches shared radio space. Nearby networks are not automatically targets because they appear in a scan. Professional work names the authorized SSID or lab network, approved hardware, capture purpose, privacy rule, and cleanup before any monitor-mode excitement.

In this lesson you will create a **wireless test card** for an authorized lab network only — ideally an isolated practice AP you own, not your neighbor’s Wi‑Fi.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-07
cd ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-07
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-07"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-07"
```

If you do not have a dedicated practice AP, complete this stage as a **planning and privacy-boundary exercise**. Do not “practice” on unknown networks.

## Start here: radio scope before capture

Wireless packets do not respect your intentions. Before enabling monitor mode or any capture tool, write:

1. Authorized SSID / BSSID
2. Channel (if known)
3. Approved adapter
4. Capture purpose
5. Privacy rule for unrelated networks and clients
6. Cleanup for temporary capture files

If those fields are blank, the card is not ready.

## Wireless fundamentals that matter for testers

| Concept | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| SSID / BSSID | Human name vs radio identity; duplicates and spoofs exist |
| Channel / band | Capture without channel focus collects irrelevant noise |
| Open / WPA2 / WPA3 | Security posture changes what “assessment” even means |
| Client vs AP | Clients may be guest phones; privacy rules still apply |
| Monitor mode | Powerful and easy to misuse outside a lab AP |

WEP cracking demos from older curricula are historical learning material. They are not a reason to attack any live network you do not own. Prefer modern lab setups where you control the AP and the clients.

## Privacy is part of scope

| Rule | Practical meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Authorized network only | Filter or ignore SSIDs that are not on the card |
| No bystander content | Do not inspect unrelated client traffic for fun |
| Purpose-bound capture | Handshake/metadata for the lab AP, not “everything in the air” |
| Retention limit | Delete captures after notes are saved unless evidence rules require keeping them |
| Location honesty | Coffee-shop airspace is not your classroom |

A strong signal from a neighbor network is still unauthorized. Signal strength is not consent.

## Wireless test card fields

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Wireless target | Authorized SSID or lab network |
| Channel | Radio channel being observed |
| Approved adapter | Hardware allowed for the lab |
| Capture purpose | Why metadata is being collected |
| Privacy rule | How unrelated networks/clients are excluded |
| Cleanup note | How temporary captures are handled |

Example:

```text
wireless_target=ASV-LAB-AP
channel=6
approved_adapter=lab wireless adapter
capture_purpose=document authorized lab handshake metadata
privacy_rule=ignore non-lab networks and unrelated clients
cleanup_note=delete temporary capture files after evidence notes are saved
```

## Assessment questions that stay honest

Good lab questions:

- Is the practice AP using the expected security mode?
- Are guest and lab SSIDs separated as intended?
- Does the lab documentation match the observed BSSID/channel?
- Are capture files stored only in the course notes workspace?

Questions that usually leave the house style:

- Can I break into the cafe Wi‑Fi?
- What is my neighbor’s password?
- Can I deauth strangers to force handshakes?

Those are not course practice tasks.

## Common beginner mistakes

- Enabling monitor mode on a laptop at home and treating every SSID as a lab
- Saving large pcaps to shared folders without review
- Running deauth floods because a tutorial showed the command
- Forgetting cleanup so captures linger on USB disks
- Calling “detected WPA2” a vulnerability by itself
- Skipping the privacy rule because “I’m only looking”

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Decide practice mode

Write one of these at the top of `wireless_test_card.txt`:

```text
practice_mode=authorized-lab-ap
```

or

```text
practice_mode=planning-only-no-capture
```

### Step 2 — Fill the card

```bash
wireless_target="ASV-LAB-AP"
channel="6"
approved_adapter="lab wireless adapter"
capture_purpose="document authorized lab handshake metadata"
privacy_rule="ignore non-lab networks and unrelated clients"
cleanup_note="delete temporary capture files after evidence notes are saved"

printf '%s\n' \
  "ssid=$wireless_target" \
  "channel=$channel" \
  "adapter=$approved_adapter" \
  "purpose=$capture_purpose" \
  "privacy=$privacy_rule" \
  "cleanup=$cleanup_note"
```

### Step 3 — Optional authorized observation

Only if `practice_mode=authorized-lab-ap` and you own/control the AP, perform the minimum observation needed for your purpose. Prefer listing the lab SSID and channel over long open-air captures. Record what you saw in `wireless_notes.txt`.

### Step 4 — Cleanup and self-review

Delete temporary captures you do not need. Ask:

- Would this card protect a bystander network?
- Is the purpose narrower than “see what happens”?
- Can I prove authorization for the SSID I named?

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| SSID | Network name advertised by an access point |
| BSSID | Radio identifier for a specific AP interface |
| Monitor mode | Adapter mode that can observe wireless frames |
| Privacy rule | Written limit that excludes unrelated networks/clients |
| Practice AP | Access point you own/control for lab learning |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] `wireless_test_card.txt` includes target, channel, adapter, purpose, privacy, cleanup
- [ ] Practice mode is explicit
- [ ] Privacy rule excludes non-lab networks
- [ ] No capture of unauthorized networks occurred
- [ ] Temporary files cleaned or planning-only status stated

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Do not assess, deauthenticate, capture, or crack networks you do not own or lack written authorization to test. Shared radio space makes mistakes easy; your card must make the boundary obvious.

When those items are true, continue to **Social Engineering Defense Testing**.

# Social Engineering Defense Testing

## Why this lesson exists

Social engineering assessments measure process and training. They can harm people if they use pressure, humiliation, credential theft, or unapproved impersonation. Professional defense testing requires approval, audience limits, safe pretexts, reporting plans, and care for the humans affected.

In this lesson you will draft a **safe simulation card** for an approved awareness exercise — not a real phishing campaign against strangers.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-08
cd ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-08
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-08"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-08"
```

You will write `safe_simulation_card.txt`. This stage is mostly planning and defense design.

## Start here: people first

Before inventing a pretext, answer:

1. What behavior are we measuring?
2. Who is in the approved audience?
3. What will the scenario refuse to do?
4. Who authorized the exercise?
5. How do results become training, not blame?

If the plan cannot protect people, it is not ready — regardless of how clever the story sounds.

## What social engineering tests can measure

| Goal | Useful signal | Harmful distortion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reporting habit | Users report suspicious training mail | Tricking users then mocking them |
| Verification habit | Users check a second channel before action | Creating fake emergencies |
| Process gaps | Help desk follows reset procedures | Pressuring staff into policy violations |
| Defense controls | Mail filters / banners catch the template | Collecting real passwords “to prove it” |

Defense testing is successful when it improves systems and training. It fails when it primarily produces embarrassment.

## Pretext boundaries that belong in writing

| Boundary | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| No credential collection | Real passwords turn training into an incident |
| No crisis impersonation | Fake medical/legal threats cause real harm |
| No executive spoofing without approval | Authority pressure warps consent |
| No targeting of excluded people | Interns, customers, or distressed staff may be off limits |
| Aggregate reporting by default | Individual gotcha lists create fear, not learning |

Feedstock material covers phishing platforms and physical techniques. In this ASV Learn path, you study those concepts through **safe planning and defense design**, not by running unauthorized campaigns.

## Safe simulation card fields

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Simulation goal | Behavior the exercise measures |
| Audience | Who is included |
| Pretext boundary | What the scenario will not claim or impersonate |
| Approval contact | Who authorized the exercise |
| Reporting plan | How results become training and remediation |

Example:

```text
simulation_goal=measure reporting of suspicious training emails
audience=approved lab cohort
pretext_boundary=no crisis claims, no credential collection, no personal pressure
approval_contact=security training owner
reporting_plan=share aggregate results and recommended awareness updates
```

## Defense notes you should write even in a lab

While drafting the simulation, also draft the defensive improvements you would recommend:

- Clear reporting button / mailbox
- Banner marking external mail
- Help-desk verification script for reset requests
- Tabletop for “urgent payment” and “urgent gift card” stories
- After-action training that avoids shaming

A simulation without a remediation path is entertainment.

## Common beginner mistakes

- Designing the cleverest lure before writing approval and audience
- Planning to collect passwords “just for metrics”
- Using fear, grief, or HR threats as pretexts
- Publishing named fail lists
- Practicing on friends/family without informed consent and a safe design
- Confusing OSINT curiosity about real people with course practice

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Choose a measurable goal

Pick one behavior, such as “report suspicious training email within one business day.”

### Step 2 — Write `safe_simulation_card.txt`

```bash
simulation_goal="measure reporting of suspicious training emails"
audience="approved lab cohort"
pretext_boundary="no crisis claims, no credential collection, no personal pressure"
approval_contact="security training owner"
reporting_plan="share aggregate results and recommended awareness updates"

printf '%s\n' \
  "goal=$simulation_goal" \
  "audience=$audience" \
  "boundary=$pretext_boundary" \
  "approval=$approval_contact" \
  "reporting=$reporting_plan"
```

### Step 3 — Write three defense recommendations

Create `defense_recommendations.txt` with three concrete controls or training updates that would make the measured behavior easier and safer.

### Step 4 — Self-review

Ask:

- Would I accept this exercise if I were in the audience?
- Does the plan avoid credential collection and crisis theater?
- Can results be reported without humiliating individuals?

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Pretext | Cover story used in a social engineering exercise |
| Audience | Approved population included in the test |
| Awareness simulation | Authorized exercise that measures human/process defenses |
| Aggregate reporting | Results summarized without unnecessary naming |
| Verification habit | Checking a second trusted channel before acting |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] `safe_simulation_card.txt` includes goal, audience, boundary, approval, reporting
- [ ] Pretext boundary forbids credential collection and crisis claims
- [ ] `defense_recommendations.txt` has at least three improvements
- [ ] No live phishing was sent to unauthorized people
- [ ] You can explain how the exercise protects participants

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Any live simulation requires explicit organizational approval outside this course page.

# Cryptography Weakness Review

## Why this lesson exists

Crypto review asks what asset is protected, what primitive is used, what weakness signal exists, how to test safely, and what remediation is practical. Beginners should not invent ciphers, log secrets for “proof,” or treat hash length as a personality quiz.

In this lesson you will write a **crypto review card** for one lab asset — for example a password verifier, TLS endpoint, or token design in your authorized training app.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-09
cd ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-09
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-09"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-09"
```

You will write `crypto_review_card.txt`. Prefer reviewing configuration and metadata over collecting secrets.

## Start here: purpose before weakness claims

Name the asset and the job cryptography is supposed to do:

1. What is being protected?
2. Is the goal confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, or password verification?
3. What primitive or protocol appears to be in use?
4. What signal suggests a weak decision?
5. How can you review it without exposing secrets?
6. What standard migration path exists?

If you cannot name the purpose, you are not ready to call the design unsafe.

## Primitive families without the folklore

| Family | Typical job | Beginner review focus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Symmetric encryption | Confidentiality with a shared key | Key handling, mode misuse, hard-coded keys |
| Asymmetric encryption / signatures | Key exchange, identity, non-repudiation clues | Certificate validity, algorithm choices |
| Hashing | Integrity fingerprints, content addressing | Collision-prone legacy hashes used as security controls |
| Password hashing | Verifying secrets at rest | Fast hashes, missing salts, no work factor |
| TLS / HTTPS | Protecting data in transit | Protocol version, cipher suite, cert trust |

Classical cipher demos (Caesar, Vigenère) are historical teaching aids. They are not modern controls. Do not “upgrade” a lab by inventing a custom mix of XOR and hope.

## Weakness signals worth documenting

| Signal | Why it matters | Safer review method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MD5/SHA-1 for password storage | Too fast / obsolete for password verification | Inspect config or code paths; do not harvest user passwords |
| Missing unique salts | Same passwords produce same hashes | Review storage format/metadata |
| TLS 1.0 / weak ciphers offered | Downgrade and compatibility risk | Use a lab TLS checker against your app |
| Hard-coded keys in source | Anyone with the repo gets the secret | Static review of lab code you own |
| Homegrown “encryption” | Usually confidentiality theater | Compare to established library guidance |

## Crypto review card fields

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Asset name | What the cryptography protects |
| Crypto use | Hashing, encryption, signing, or verification |
| Weakness signal | Clue that a decision may be unsafe |
| Safe test method | How to review without exposing secrets |
| Remediation note | Safer standard or migration path |

Example:

```text
asset_name=student password verifier
crypto_use=password hashing for verification
weakness_signal=unsalted fast hash observed in legacy records
safe_test_method=review configuration and sample metadata without collecting passwords
remediation_note=migrate to slow password hashing with unique salts
```

## TLS review in the lab

If your authorized lab app speaks HTTPS, a useful beginner review is:

```bash
# Example only — use your lab hostname
openssl s_client -connect lab.local:443 -servername lab.local </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -subject -issuer
```

Record protocol expectations, certificate subject, validity window, and whether the cert matches the lab hostname. Do not turn this into internet-wide scanning.

## Common beginner mistakes

- Inventing a custom cipher “for learning”
- Logging secrets or private keys into notes shared to cloud sync
- Calling Base64 encryption
- Reusing one salt “to keep things simple”
- Equating “HTTPS present” with “crypto is done”
- Running password-cracking tools against real user databases outside a dedicated lab story

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Pick one lab asset

Choose a password verifier, token, TLS endpoint, or file encryption setting you control.

### Step 2 — Write `crypto_review_card.txt`

```bash
asset_name="student password verifier"
crypto_use="password hashing for verification"
weakness_signal="unsalted fast hash observed in legacy records"
safe_test_method="review configuration and sample metadata without collecting passwords"
remediation_note="migrate to slow password hashing with unique salts"

printf '%s\n' \
  "asset=$asset_name" \
  "use=$crypto_use" \
  "signal=$weakness_signal" \
  "test=$safe_test_method" \
  "remediation=$remediation_note"
```

### Step 3 — Optional safe lab check

If you have a local HTTPS training app, capture certificate metadata only. If not, document the review method you would use and stop at planning.

### Step 4 — Self-review

Ask:

- Did I name purpose before weakness?
- Did my method avoid collecting secrets?
- Is remediation a recognized standard, not a custom invention?

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Primitive | Established cryptographic building block |
| Password hashing | Slow, salted verification of secrets at rest |
| TLS | Protocol family protecting data in transit |
| Weakness signal | Observable clue that a crypto decision may be unsafe |
| Migration path | Practical move toward a stronger standard |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] `crypto_review_card.txt` includes asset, use, signal, safe method, remediation
- [ ] Safe method avoids collecting passwords or private keys
- [ ] Remediation names an established approach
- [ ] No custom cipher was proposed as a fix
- [ ] Any live check stayed on the lab asset

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Review cryptography on systems you own or are authorized to assess. Do not attempt to break cryptography on third-party services as “practice.”

When those items are true, continue to **Cloud Security Assessment**.

# Cloud Security Assessment

## Why this lesson exists

Cloud testing is mostly configuration and evidence review. The approved account, identity boundary, storage checks, logging signals, and remediation owner matter more than flashy exploit demos. Many real cloud incidents start as misconfiguration, not movie hacking.

In this lesson you will write a **cloud assessment row** for an authorized training project/account — or a planning row if you are using local mocks and documentation only.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-10
cd ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-10
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-10"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-10"
```

You will write `cloud_assessment_row.txt`. Keep provider credentials out of git and out of lesson screenshots.

## Start here: cloud scope before configuration review

Write the boundary first:

1. Which account, subscription, or project is approved?
2. Which identities/roles are in review?
3. Which storage or network controls are being checked?
4. Which logs prove monitoring exists?
5. Who owns the fix?
6. What is explicitly out of scope (other accounts, customer tenancies, production)?

Cloud power makes cross-account mistakes expensive. Scope is the safety rail.

## Shared responsibility without slogans

| Layer | Provider usually owns | Customer / lab owner usually owns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Physical data centers | Facilities and hardware controls | Almost nothing here |
| Managed service runtime | Platform patching for the service | Configuration of the service |
| Identity and access | IAM features | Who gets which role |
| Data | Encryption features | Classification, key choices, exposure settings |
| Logging | Log products | Enabling, retention, review, response |

A managed database being “in the cloud” does not mean the provider chose your public exposure settings for you.

## High-value misconfiguration themes

| Theme | Lab review question | Evidence to capture |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Storage exposure | Is the bucket/container private by default policy? | Policy JSON / console evidence, not downloaded private data |
| IAM excess | Does a lab role allow `*` on sensitive actions? | Role policy summary |
| Network exposure | Are admin ports open to the world? | Security group / firewall rules |
| Secrets in code | Are keys committed to a lab repo? | File path and redacted snippet |
| Logging gaps | Are admin actions audited? | Log config enabled/disabled |

If you find a publicly listable training bucket in your own authorized cloud lab account, document exposure settings. Do not download other people’s data if you stumble into something unexpected — stop and fix ownership assumptions.

## Cloud assessment row fields

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Cloud account scope | Approved account, subscription, or project |
| Identity boundary | Roles and permissions in review |
| Storage check | Exposure or encryption evidence inspected |
| Logging signal | Logs that prove monitoring exists |
| Remediation owner | Who owns the fix |

Example:

```text
cloud_account_scope=asv-training-project
identity_boundary=review lab roles only
storage_check=confirm private buckets and encryption settings
logging_signal=cloud audit log enabled for admin actions
remediation_owner=cloud platform owner
```

## Containers and Kubernetes as cloud-adjacent scope

If your lab includes containers:

- Review whether the container runs as root unnecessarily
- Check whether secrets are baked into images
- Confirm network policies are intentional
- Keep cluster credentials out of notes that sync publicly

Treat cluster names like hostnames: only touch labeled lab clusters.

## Common beginner mistakes

- Scanning the public internet for open buckets as homework
- Using personal cloud root credentials for experiments
- Screenshotting full access keys into chat
- Calling “cloud” a finding without naming the control
- Testing a workplace cloud account without written permission
- Ignoring logging because storage findings feel more exciting

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Declare practice mode

```text
practice_mode=authorized-cloud-lab-account
```

or

```text
practice_mode=planning-only
```

### Step 2 — Write `cloud_assessment_row.txt`

```text
cloud_account_scope=asv-training-project
identity_boundary=review lab roles only
storage_check=confirm private buckets and encryption settings
logging_signal=cloud audit log enabled for admin actions
remediation_owner=cloud platform owner
out_of_scope=any cloud account not named in this row
```

Optional shell print:

```bash
cloud_account_scope="asv-training-project"
identity_boundary="review lab roles only"
storage_check="confirm private buckets and encryption settings"
logging_signal="cloud audit log enabled for admin actions"
remediation_owner="cloud platform owner"

printf '%s\n' \
  "scope=$cloud_account_scope" \
  "identity=$identity_boundary" \
  "storage=$storage_check" \
  "logging=$logging_signal" \
  "owner=$remediation_owner"
```

### Step 3 — Collect one evidence note

If you have an authorized cloud lab account, export or copy one non-secret configuration evidence item (for example: “bucket public access block = on”). If planning-only, write the exact console/CLI check you would run.

### Step 4 — Self-review

Ask:

- Is the account scope unmistakable?
- Did I avoid collecting foreign data?
- Does an owner exist for the remediation?

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Shared responsibility | Split of security duties between provider and customer |
| IAM | Identity and access management |
| Misconfiguration | Unsafe settings that create exposure without a novel exploit |
| Audit log | Record of administrative or data-plane actions |
| Sandbox account | Isolated cloud project approved for learning |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] Practice mode is explicit
- [ ] `cloud_assessment_row.txt` includes scope, identity, storage, logging, owner
- [ ] Evidence note avoids secrets and foreign data
- [ ] Out-of-scope accounts are named
- [ ] No public-bucket hunting on the open internet

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Do not probe random public buckets “to learn.”

Assess only cloud accounts and projects you own or are explicitly authorized to test. Public exposure on the internet is not an invitation.

When those items are true, continue to **Mobile Security Review**.

# Mobile Security Review

## Why this lesson exists

Mobile security review focuses on app behavior, permissions, storage, network use, and data handling inside an approved test setup. A test device or emulator, synthetic data, and one clear permission question keep the review controlled.

In this lesson you will write a **mobile review card** for an approved lab app package — or a planning card if you do not have an emulator ready yet.

## Reminder: where you work

```bash
mkdir -p ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-11
cd ~/asv-learn-ethical-hacking/stage-11
```

Windows (PowerShell):

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-11"
Set-Location "$HOME\asv-learn-ethical-hacking\stage-11"
```

You will write `mobile_review_card.txt`. Keep personal phone backups and real contacts out of the exercise.

## Start here: test device before app claims

Before inspecting an app, write:

1. App package / build label
2. Test device or emulator
3. Data handling rule
4. Permission or storage question under review
5. What evidence would support a reportable issue
6. What is out of scope (production accounts, real SMS, friend devices)

Mobile platforms make it easy to touch real identity data. Your card must forbid that explicitly.

## Platform ideas without tool worship

| Area | Review question | Evidence examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Permissions | Does the feature need this permission now? | Permission list vs feature map |
| Local storage | Are tokens or PII stored in predictable world-readable places? | Storage path notes on a lab build |
| Transport | Does the lab build pin or at least require TLS? | Proxy notes against the lab app |
| Auth session | What happens on logout / token expiry? | Observed session behavior |
| WebViews | Is untrusted content executed with too much power? | Navigation and JS bridge notes |
| IoT-adjacent apps | Does the companion app expose device admin carelessly? | Pairing and local network notes |

Deep tooling (Frida, Objection, firmware extraction) appears in feedstock. In this course stage, mastery means **one controlled review question with synthetic data**, not a full mobile exploit pipeline.

## Synthetic data rules

| Allowed | Not allowed |
| --- | --- |
| Fake names and lab emails | Real customer or family data |
| Throwaway lab accounts | Production SSO accounts |
| Sample tokens generated for the lab | Stolen session cookies from real apps |
| Screenshots of lab-only screens | Photos of other people’s private content |

If the only way to test a feature is to use real personal data, redesign the lab or stop.

## Mobile review card fields

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| App package | Approved app build or package name |
| Test device | Device or emulator used for the lab |
| Data handling rule | What test data can be used |
| Permission review | Which permissions are being checked |
| Finding note | What evidence would support a reportable issue |

Example:

```text
app_package=lab.training.mobile
test_device=approved lab emulator
data_handling_rule=use synthetic accounts and no personal data
permission_review=compare requested permissions to the app feature need
finding_note=document permission, evidence, impact, and remediation
```

## A simple review workflow

1. Install only the lab build on the lab emulator/device.
2. List permissions and map each to a feature.
3. Exercise one feature with synthetic data.
4. Note storage or network behaviors that seem excessive.
5. Write one finding note or an explicit “no issue evidenced” note.
6. Uninstall or reset the emulator snapshot when done.

“No issue evidenced” is a valid professional outcome.

## Common beginner mistakes

- Sideloading random APKs from the internet onto a daily-driver phone
- Using a personal Google/Apple account full of real data
- Calling every permission “malware”
- Proxying all phone traffic without noticing non-lab apps
- Publishing lab package names as if they were vendor 0-days
- Skipping uninstall/reset so lab credentials linger

## Your local task

### Step 1 — Declare practice mode

```text
practice_mode=lab-emulator
```

or

```text
practice_mode=planning-only
```

### Step 2 — Write `mobile_review_card.txt`

```bash
app_package="lab.training.mobile"
test_device="approved lab emulator"
data_handling_rule="use synthetic accounts and no personal data"
permission_review="compare requested permissions to the app feature need"
finding_note="document permission, evidence, impact, and remediation"

printf '%s\n' \
  "app=$app_package" \
  "device=$test_device" \
  "data_rule=$data_handling_rule" \
  "permissions=$permission_review" \
  "finding=$finding_note"
```

### Step 3 — Permission map

Create `permission_map.txt` with at least three permissions (real from your lab app, or realistic examples if planning-only) and whether each is justified by a feature.

### Step 4 — Self-review

Ask:

- Is all data synthetic?
- Is the device a lab device?
- Does the finding note require evidence, not vibes?

## Key vocabulary

| Term | Meaning here |
| --- | --- |
| Package name | Application identifier on the platform |
| Emulator | Virtual device used for safer lab testing |
| Permission | OS-mediated access to sensitive capabilities |
| Synthetic data | Fake data created for testing |
| Companion app | Mobile app that controls or monitors a device |

## Proof checklist

- [ ] Practice mode is explicit
- [ ] `mobile_review_card.txt` complete
- [ ] `permission_map.txt` has at least three rows
- [ ] Data handling rule forbids personal/production data
- [ ] No review of unauthorized third-party production apps as “practice targets”

## ASV Learn house notes

Practice runs in your own lab (local terminal, VM, or authorized lab hosts). ASV Learn hosts the lesson text; keep scope legal and document evidence yourself.

Review only app builds and devices you are authorized to test. Do not reverse or intercept other people’s production apps or accounts for this course.

When those items are true, continue to **Reporting & Remediation**.
